source_terms: Before an ad is made at great cost, the agency always gets a 'storyboard', which is a pictorial depiction of the ad, approved by the Doordarshan authorities.

item.claim: Under Doordarshan, clearance ran as two separate gates: a storyboard was approved before production, and the finished film was approved again afterwards. Approval at the first gate did not bind the second. The author reports his own Sweetex campaign clearing the storyboard and then being rejected on the finished film for showing the model's navel in an opening close-up, forcing a reshoot at the advertiser's cost.

mechanism.text: The storyboard is a pictorial abstraction; the finished film contains framing, duration and emphasis that the storyboard does not fix. A censor assessing the film is therefore assessing material the storyboard never showed, and can reach a different verdict on the same concept.

scope.conditions: India, mid-1980s, state-monopoly television. The two-gate structure described is Doordarshan-era and the author reports the rules "kept changing". It must not be read as current Indian practice.

caveats.text: the author is a participant recounting a grievance thirty years later; the reasoning attributed to the Doordarshan official is his recollection of a conversation

item.visible_content: Four panels in two rows. Left of each row, a poster for the same event — a Hear-Say reading by Henry Magaziner at a Philadelphia bookshop, with the same date, time and address. Right of each row, the alignment structure that composition implies, drawn as teal rules. Top row: the information is set as one flush-right stack, and the derived structure is two fields divided by a single vertical axis. Bottom row: the same information is broken into several differently-weighted groups scattered across the format, and the derived structure is a multi-field grid of roughly five vertical and five horizontal divisions.
item.what_the_visual_supports: That a grid is READ OFF a composition rather than imposed on it. The content is held constant and only the grouping changes, and the structure changes with it. It also supports the source's narrower claim that a large variety of layouts is reachable inside strict limits: both posters use one type family and a small set of sizes.
item.requires_prose: That like information is grouped and disparate information separated, and that changes in weight and scale are what introduce hierarchy. The picture shows the outcome; the caption supplies the rule that produced it.
item.extractor_note: This is the clearest minimal pair in the section — same content, one variable (grouping) changed, both results shown with their derived structures. The caption states the claim, so a text-only extraction keeps the claim and loses the proof.

item.definition_in_origin_frame: Specifying a reduced offer by removing what the supplier's own product hierarchy treats as inessential, when the buyer's reference set is a different one. Named from the source's line: "What suppliers consider to be a frill, consumers consider to be a necessity."

item.question: A 20-second ad for a new energy drink opens on a silent slow-motion product beauty shot, brings the logo up only at the very end, shows no people at all, and closes on a "Buy now" end card. The brief is an awareness campaign. Judged strictly by this source, what is wrong with it — and what is not?
item.answer: Three of the four awareness instructions are missed. Attention for awareness is to be won with audio ("Pump up the volume by using audio to get viewers to pay attention") and the opening is silent. Branding is to be "front and center" and the brand arrives last, which also fails the core guideline to show up early and throughout. Connection is to "Make the people core to the story", and there are no people, which also fails the core guideline to humanise the story. What is not wrong on this source's terms is the end card: awareness is the one row where Direction is left at "Apply core principles", and the core guidance asks only that a CTA be present and intentionally chosen for a specific objective. The source gives no basis for calling the ask misplaced or over-strong here, and asserting one would go beyond it.
item.support: Awareness row: audio-led attention, brand front and centre, people core to the story, Direction at core. Core rows supply the early-and-throughout and humanise guidelines.
confounders: criticising the 'Buy now' CTA as wrong for awareness — a reasonable marketing instinct that this source does not support

source_terms: lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot
the great Indian rope trick of numbers
item.claim: Bijapurkar states the structural claim on which most of the book rests: "Consumer demand in the emerging economies is made up of lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot," where developed-market marketers "are used to working with an exactly opposite demand structure — a few people consuming a lot each, adding up to a lot." She draws the consequence explicitly: "neither the pricing paradigms nor the cost structures of their usual, tried and tested global business models are appropriate for India's demand structure." She names the counter-intuitive consequence the "great Indian rope trick of numbers" — a small penetration of a large population produces a large absolute market, so lower-income groups can out-consume higher-income groups in absolute terms.

mechanism.text: Business models encode assumptions about consumption per head. A retail format sized for a catchment that consumes a lot per head will not reach viability in a catchment that consumes little per head, regardless of how many people are in it — which is why, on her account, the first organised retail forays failed and why a small-format chain with an aggregated back end succeeded by "mimicking the structure of the customer demand".

scope.conditions: Stated for India and for emerging markets more generally, on data to 2008. Bijapurkar draws the general form from the BRIC comparison — economies "individually poor but collectively rich" — and cites Goldman Sachs's *Dreaming with the BRICs*.

caveats.text: the two-wheeler evidence was inspected and it holds. Figure 4.1 (rural two-wheeler market) shows penetration falling 42 / 25 / 10 / 2.7 per cent across income groups while household counts rise 7 / 18 / 63 / 66 million, giving two-wheeler numbers of 3.8 / 4.5 / 6.4 / 1.8 million. The lower-middle group therefore does have about 1.6 times the units of the high-income group, exactly as the text claims. Source: Indian Readership Survey 2008

the general claim about business models is argued from a small number of Indian cases (Subhiksha, shampoo sachets, community telephony) with no failure cases and no financial detail. Subhiksha in particular is presented as a success; the chain collapsed shortly after this edition was published, which the book could not know and which is recorded here because the case is load-bearing
SEVERE FRESHNESS RISK. Every figure supporting this object is 2008 or earlier and predates mobile data, e-commerce and digital payments in India

item.source_locator: Essay 'SRK – Brand Ambassador for the Market'
item.question: What is this source's reading of Shah Rukh Khan, and why does the extraction refuse to turn it into a casting principle?
item.answer: That he embodies rather than merely uses market forces: a figure demonstrating that fame, fortune, success and family can be had together and easily; whose Raj/Rahul characters made modernity desirable by presenting it as a distillation of tradition rather than a break from it; and who is consumed as himself playing a character rather than as an actor disappearing into one. The extraction refuses to turn it into a casting principle because it is film and cultural criticism throughout — every element is the author's interpretation of films and of a public persona, and no audience evidence of any kind is offered for what 'people seem to want'. Converting criticism into production advice is exactly the failure this record avoids. It is retained because it is the corpus's only material on how an Indian star persona is read culturally.
item.support: 'he plays himself, or more accurately, plays Shah Rukh Khan playing the character'
item.confounders: The reading is compelling and entirely unevidenced; those two facts are independent.

item.label: why_indian_advertising_became_saturated_with_celebrities
item.description: The four reasons the author himself gives, in one passage, for the saturation of Indian advertising with film and cricket stars: celebrity cost is small relative to media weight; celebrity credibility helps drive categories down the socio-economic pyramid; the corporatisation of the film industry made stars available; and pre-testing rewards celebrity presence.

whole_system_claim.text: Celebrity saturation is over-determined: several independent forces each push the same way, so no single one of them needs to be the cause, and at least one of them — the pre-test — pushes for reasons unconnected to whether the advertising works.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The author does list these as reasons, in sequence, in one passage ("The answer may lie somewhere else… The second reason is… One final reason…"), so the membership and the ordering are his. What is the extractor's is the over-determination claim: the observation that the forces are independent of one another and that this makes the phenomenon insensitive to any one of them. The author draws no such conclusion.
whole_system_claim.source_ref: Ch. 'Meri Khubsurti Ka Raaz', 'Why this celebrity obsession, you may ask.'

evidence.system_level_uncertainty:
Moderate. The membership and sequence are the source's own — he enumerates the reasons — so unlike the other three systems here the grouping is not invented. The over-determination reading is the extractor's.

A RECORDED CONFLICT BETWEEN sk_nnn_0041 AND sk_nnn_0042 WAS REMOVED IN THE CANON-014 FINAL RECONCILIATION, and the tension it pointed at is kept here as prose because it is real and the conflict edge was not. sk_nnn_0042 reports a study concluding that a celebrity's aura dominates; sk_nnn_0041 reports that agencies began casting stars as characters once mere celebrity endorsement stopped differentiating. Those two statements create a tension worth noticing and they do not contradict each other: a performer can carry high aura AND be deliberately cast as a character, and on the source's own account the second practice exists precisely because the first became universal and therefore stopped distinguishing one advertiser from another. Encoding that as a structural `conflict` asserted a logical incompatibility the source does not contain and the statements do not support. What the source genuinely does is state both without reconciling them, which is recorded here and is an observation about the source rather than a defect in the knowledge.

item.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Above average', item 3 (spine 14)
item.question: You are casting a testimonial commercial and have found a genuine loyal customer who happens to be an excellent, polished speaker. What does Ogilvy say about that, and what device does he recommend for producing conviction?
item.answer: He tells you to avoid users who would give so polished a performance that viewers would think they were professional actors, on the stated ground that the more amateurish the performance, the more credible it is. The device he recommends is to have the interviewer pretend to find fault with the product so that the loyal user rises to its defence, which he says produces far more conviction than simply asking what the user thinks — and he prefers filming users who do not know they are being filmed. The mechanism is that credibility comes from the speaker appearing not to be performing for the advertiser, and both clumsiness and spontaneous defence are signals of that.
item.support: Stated rule with a reproduced hidden-camera script and one supporting case — a French campaign whose elderly heroine became recognised by three in four people, with the product reported to have moved from fourth to second in sales. The recognition figure is measured; the rank change is attributed with nothing else excluded.
confounders: assuming production polish always helps; his claim runs the other way for this specific format
reading it as an argument for using real people generally, missing the defensive-response device
confusing this with his position on expert testimony, which works through standing rather than through amateurism
